verses.zh: （大卫的诗，交与伶长。调用慕拉便。）我要一心称谢耶和华；我要传扬你一切奇妙的作为。
verses.en: For the music director, according to the alumoth-labben style;[NOTE:1] a psalm of David.I will thank the Lord with all my heart!I will tell about all your amazing deeds.[NOTE:2]
notes: Psalm 9. The psalmist, probably speaking on behalf of Israel or Judah, praises God for delivering him from hostile nations. He celebrates God’s sovereignty and justice, and calls on others to join him in boasting of God’s greatness. Many Hebrew mss and the ancient Greek version (LXX) combine Psalms 9 and 10 into a single psalm.

The meaning of the Hebrew term עַלְמוּת (’almut) is uncertain. Some mss divide the form into עַל מוּת (’al mut, “according to the death [of the son]”), while the LXX assumes a reading עַל עֲלֻמוֹת (’al ’alumot, “according to alumoth”). The phrase probably refers to a particular tune or musical style.

verses.zh: 我要因你欢喜快乐；至高者啊，我要歌颂你的名！
verses.en: I will be happy and rejoice in you.I will sing praises to you, O Most High.[NOTE:1]
notes: The cohortative forms in vv. 1-2 express the psalmist’s resolve to praise God publicly.

verses.zh: 我的仇敌转身退去的时候，他们一见你的面就跌倒灭亡。
verses.en: When my enemies turn back,they trip and are defeated[NOTE:1] before you.
notes: Heb “[to] your name, O Most High.” God’s “name” refers metonymically to his divine characteristics as suggested by his name, in this case “Most High.” This divine title (עֶלְיוֹן, ʿelyon) pictures God as the exalted ruler of the universe who vindicates the innocent and judges the wicked. See especially Ps 47:2.

verses.zh: 因你已经为我伸冤，为我辨屈；你坐在宝座上，按公义审判。
verses.en: For you defended my just cause;[NOTE:1] from your throne you pronounced a just decision.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “perish”; or “die.” The imperfect verbal forms in this line either emphasize what typically happens or describe vividly the aftermath of a recent battle in which the Lord defeated the psalmist’s enemies.
Heb “for you accomplished my justice and my legal claim.”

verses.zh: 你曾斥责外邦，你曾灭绝恶人；你曾涂抹他们的名，直到永永远远。
verses.en: You terrified the nations with your battle cry.[NOTE:1] You destroyed the wicked;[NOTE:2] you permanently wiped out all memory of them.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “you sat on a throne [as] one who judges [with] righteousness.” The perfect verbal forms in v. 4 probably allude to a recent victory (see vv. 5-7). Another option is to understand the verbs as describing what is typical (“you defend…you sit on a throne”).

The verb גָּעַר (gaʿar) is often understood to mean “rebuke” and in this context taken to refer to the Lord’s “rebuke” of the nations. In some cases it is apparent that scolding or threatening is in view (see Gen 37:10; Ruth 2:16; Zech 3:2). However, in militaristic contexts this translation is inadequate, for the verb refers in this setting to the warrior’s battle cry, which terrifies and paralyzes the enemy. See A. Caquot, TDOT 3:53, and note the use of the verb in Pss 68:30; 106:9; and Nah 1:4, as well as the related noun in Job 26:11; Pss 18:15; 76:6; 104:7; Isa 50:2; 51:20; 66:15.

The singular form is collective (note “nations” and “their name”). In the psalms the “wicked” (רְשָׁעִים, reshaʿim) are typically proud, practical atheists (Ps 10:2, 4, 11) who hate God’s commands, commit sinful deeds, speak lies and slander (Ps 50:16-20), and cheat others (Ps 37:21). In this context the hostile nations who threaten Israel/Judah are in view.

verses.zh: 仇敌到了尽头；他们被毁坏，直到永远。你拆毁他们的城邑，连他们的名号都归于无有。
verses.en: The enemy’s cities have been reduced to permanent ruins.[NOTE:1] You destroyed their cities;[NOTE:2] all memory of the enemies has perished.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “their name you wiped out forever and ever.” The three perfect verbal forms in v. 5 probably refer to a recent victory (definite past or present perfect use), although they might express what is typical (characteristic use).

Heb “the enemy—they have come to an end [in] ruins permanently.” The singular form אוֹיֵב (ʾoyev, “enemy”) is collective. It is placed at the beginning of the verse to heighten the contrast with יְהוָה (yehvah, “the Lord”) in v. 7.
Heb “you uprooted cities.”

verses.zh: 惟耶和华坐着为王，直到永远；他已经为审判设摆他的宝座。
verses.en: But the Lord[NOTE:1] rules[NOTE:2] forever;he reigns in a just manner.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “it has perished, their remembrance, they.” The independent pronoun at the end of the line is in apposition to the preceding pronominal suffix and lends emphasis (see IBHS 299 §16.3.4). The referent of the masculine pronoun is the nations/enemies (cf. v. 5), not the cities (the Hebrew noun עָרִים [ʿarim, “cities”] is grammatically feminine). This has been specified in the present translation for clarity; many modern translations retain the pronoun “them,” resulting in ambiguity (cf. NRSV “their cities you have rooted out; the very memory of them has perished”).
The construction vav (ו) + subject highlights the contrast between the exalted Lord and his defeated foes (see v. 6).
Heb “sits” (i.e., enthroned, see v. 4). The imperfect verbal form highlights the generalization.

verses.zh: 他要按公义审判世界，按正直判断万民。
verses.en: He judges the world fairly;he makes just legal decisions for the nations.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “he establishes for justice his throne.”

verses.zh: 耶和华又要给受欺压的人作高台，在患难的时候作高台。
verses.en: Consequently[NOTE:1] the Lord provides safety for the oppressed;[NOTE:2] he provides safety in times of trouble.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “the peoples.” The imperfect verbal forms in v. 8 either describe God’s typical, characteristic behavior, or anticipate a future judgment of worldwide proportions (“will judge…”).

Following the imperfect in v. 9, the construction vav (ו) conjunctive + shortened form of the prefixed verb הָיָה (hayah) indicates a consequence or result of the preceding statement. The construction functions this same way in Pss 81:15 and 104:20.
Heb “and the Lord is an elevated place for the oppressed.” The singular form דָּךְ (dakh, “oppressed”) is collective here.

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，认识你名的人要倚靠你，因你没有离弃寻求你的人。
verses.en: Your loyal followers trust in you,[NOTE:1] for you, Lord, do not abandon those who seek your help.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “[he is] an elevated place for times in trouble.” Here an “elevated place” refers to a stronghold, a defensible, secure position that represents a safe haven in times of unrest or distress (cf. NEB “tower of strength”; NIV, NRSV “stronghold”).

Heb “and the ones who know your name trust in you.” The construction vav (ו) conjunctive + imperfect at the beginning of the verse expresses another consequence of the statement made in v. 8. “To know” the Lord’s “name” means to be his follower, recognizing his authority and maintaining loyalty to him. See Ps 91:14, where “knowing” the Lord’s “name” is associated with loving him.

verses.zh: 应当歌颂居锡安的耶和华，将他所行的传扬在众民中。
verses.en: Sing praises to the Lord, who rules[NOTE:1] in Zion.Tell the nations what he has done.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “the ones who seek you.”
Heb “sits” (i.e., enthroned, and therefore ruling—see v. 4). Another option is to translate as “lives” or “dwells.”

verses.zh: 因为那追讨流人血之罪的―他记念受屈的人，不忘记困苦人的哀求。
verses.en: For the one who takes revenge against murderers took notice of the oppressed;[NOTE:1] he did not overlook[NOTE:2] their cry for help[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “declare among the nations his deeds.”

Heb “for the one who seeks shed blood remembered them.” The idiomatic expression “to seek shed blood” seems to carry the idea “to seek payment/restitution for one’s shed blood.” The plural form דָּמִים (damim, “shed blood”) occurs only here as the object of דָּרַשׁ (darash, “to seek”); the singular form דָּם (dam, “blood”) appears with the verb in Gen 9:5; 42:22; Ezek 33:6. “Them,” the pronominal object of the verb “remembered,” refers to the oppressed, mentioned specifically in the next line, so the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “did not forget.”

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，你是从死门把我提拔起来的；求你怜恤我，看那恨我的人所加给我的苦难，
verses.en: when they prayed:[NOTE:1] “Have mercy on me,[NOTE:2] Lord!See how I am oppressed by those who hate me,[NOTE:3] O one who can snatch me away[NOTE:4] from the gates of death!
notes: Heb “the cry for help of the oppressed.” In this context the “oppressed” are the psalmist and those he represents, whom the hostile nations have threatened.

The words “when they prayed,” though not represented in the Hebrew text, are supplied in the translation for clarification. The petition in vv. 13-14 is best understood as the cry for help which the oppressed offered to God when the nations threatened. The Lord answered this request, prompting the present song of thanksgiving.
Or “show me favor.”
Heb “see my misery from the ones who hate me.”

verses.zh: 好叫我述说你一切的美德；我必在锡安城（原文是女子）的门因你的救恩欢乐。
verses.en: Then I will[NOTE:1] tell about all your praiseworthy acts;[NOTE:2] in the gates of Daughter Zion[NOTE:3] I will rejoice because of your deliverance.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “one who lifts me up.”
Or “so that I might.”
Heb “all your praise.” “Praise” stands by metonymy for the mighty acts that prompt it.
Daughter Zion is an idiomatic title for Jerusalem. It appears frequently in the prophets, but only here in the psalms.

verses.zh: 外邦人陷在自己所掘的坑中；他们的脚在自己暗设的网罗里缠住了。
verses.en: The nations fell[NOTE:1] into the pit they had made;their feet were caught in the net they had hidden.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “in your deliverance.”
Heb “sank down.”

verses.zh: 耶和华已将自己显明了，他已施行审判；恶人被自己手所做的缠住了（或译：他叫恶人被自己手所做的累住了）。（细拉）
verses.en: The Lord revealed himself;he accomplished justice.The wicked were ensnared by their own actions.[NOTE:1] (Higgaion.[NOTE:2] Selah)
notes: The hostility of the nations against God’s people is their downfall, for it prompts God to intervene and destroy them. See also Ps 7:15-16.

Heb “by the work of his hands [the] wicked [one] was ensnared.” The singular form רָשָׁע (rashaʿ, “wicked”) is collective or representative here (see vv. 15, 17). The form נוֹקֵשׁ (noqesh) appears to be an otherwise unattested Qal form (active participle) from נָקַשׁ (naqash), but the form should be emended to נוֹקַשׁ (noqash), a Niphal perfect from יָקַשׁ (yaqash).

verses.zh: 恶人，就是忘记　神的外邦人，都必归到阴间。
verses.en: The wicked are turned back and sent to Sheol;[NOTE:1] this is the destiny of[NOTE:2] all the nations that ignore[NOTE:3] God,
notes: This is probably a technical musical term.
Heb “the wicked turn back to Sheol.” The imperfect verbal form either emphasizes what typically happens or describes vividly the aftermath of the Lord’s victory over the psalmist’s enemies. See v. 3.
The words “this is the destiny of” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. The verb “are turned back” is understood by ellipsis (see the preceding line).

verses.zh: 穷乏人必不永久被忘；困苦人的指望必不永远落空。
verses.en: for the needy are not permanently ignored,[NOTE:1] the hopes of the oppressed are not forever dashed.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “forget.” “Forgetting God” refers here to worshiping false gods and thereby refusing to recognize his sovereignty (see also Deut 8:19; Judg 3:7; 1 Sam 12:9; Isa 17:10; Jer 3:21; Ps 44:20). The nations’ refusal to acknowledge God’s sovereignty accounts for their brazen attempt to attack and destroy his people.
Or “forgotten.”

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你起来，不容人得胜！愿外邦人在你面前受审判！
verses.en: Rise up, Lord![NOTE:1] Don’t let men be defiant.[NOTE:2] May the nations be judged in your presence.
notes: Heb “the hope of the afflicted does [not] perish forever.” The negative particle is understood by ellipsis; note the preceding line. The imperfect verbal forms express what typically happens.
Rise up, Lord!…May the nations be judged. The psalm concludes with a petition that the Lord would continue to exercise his justice as he has done in the recent crisis.

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你使外邦人恐惧；愿他们知道自己不过是人。（细拉）
verses.en: Terrify them, Lord.[NOTE:1] Let the nations know they are mere mortals.[NOTE:2] (Selah)
notes: Or “prevail.”

Heb “place, Lord, terror with regard to them.” The Hebrew term מוֹרָה (morah, “terror”) is an alternative form of מוֹרָא (moraʾ; a reading that appears in some mss and finds support in several ancient textual witnesses).

READING CYCLE THREE(see "Guide
to Good Bible Reading")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT
PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means
that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of
us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are
priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3).
Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above.
Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original
author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has
one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- For a brief discussion of MT superscripts, see Introduction to the Psalms, IV. Authorship.

- The New Jerusalem Bible (NJB) asserts that Psalm 9 and Psalm 10 form a loose acrostic (cf. LXX).

- Acrostics are a specialized type of poetry. In order to make each letter fit

- rare words used

- rare forms of words used

- strained lines of poetry occur

- unusual metaphors and figurative language occur

- use of PREPOSITIONS

The ancients felt the alphabet had magical significance (i.e., Kabala, Ras
Shamra texts).

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: PSALM 9:1-2
1I
will give thanks to the Lord with all my
heart;
I will tell of all
Your wonders.
2I
will be glad and exult in You;
I
will sing praise to Your name, O Most High.

9:1-2 This opening strophe has five COHORTATIVES.

- I will give thanks – BDB 392, KB 389, Hiphil IMPERFECT
used in a COHORTATIVE sense

- I will tell – BDB 707, KB 765, Piel COHORTATIVE

- I will be glad – BDB 970, KB 1333, Qal COHORTATIVE

- I will exult – BDB 763, KB 836, Qal COHORTATIVE

- I will sing, praise – BDB 274, KB 273, Piel COHORTATIVE

All of these relate to YHWH (i.e., the Most High). Thanksgiving and praise
are the duty of mankind. These are signs/evidences of an intimate,
personal, daily relationship with God.

Notice the four "I wills" of Ps. 9:1-2 are based on the five
"You haves" of Ps. 9:4-6. YHWH has acted! Now His followers can
praise Him!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THANKSGIVING

9:1 "with all my heart" This was a
Hebrew idiom of complete devotion (cf. Psalm 86:12; 111:1; 138:1; 1 Kgs.
8:23,61; 11:4; 1 Chr. 28:9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

▣

NASB, NJB, JPSOA
"wonders"

NKJV, Peshitta
"marvelous works"

NRSV, REB, LXX
"wonderful deeds"

This is a Hebrew CONSTRUCT (BDB 481 and BDB
810, Niphal PARTICIPLE). This denotes God's
acts which are beyond human comprehension.

TOPIC: WONDERFUL THINGS (פלא)

9:2 "in You. . .to Your Name"
These are parallel. Notice the personal element in worship.

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: PSALM 9:3-6
3When
my enemies turn back,
They
stumble and perish before You.
4For
You have maintained my just cause;
You
have sat on the throne judging righteously.
5You have rebuked the
nations, You have destroyed the wicked;
You
have blotted out their name forever and ever.
6The enemy has come to an
end in perpetual ruins,
And
You have uprooted the cities;
The
very memory of them has perished.

9:3-6 This strophe extolls YHWH as a
Righteous Judge (cf. Ps. 9:4b).

Notice His actions toward the enemy (i.e., YHWH as Israel's Divine Warrior).

- enemies turn back, Ps. 9:3a – BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT (i.e., in battle)

- enemies stumble, Ps. 9:3b – BDB 505, KB 502, Niphal IMPERFECT

- enemies perish, Ps. 9:3b – BDB 1, KB 2, Qal IMPERFECT

- has rebuked the nations, Ps. 9:5a – BDB 172, KB 199, Qal PERFECT
(NET Bible sees this as referring to a "battle cry," p. 858, #19)

- has destroyed the wicked, Ps. 9:5a – BDB 1, KB 2, Piel PERFECT

- has blotted out their name, Ps. 9:5b – BDB 562, KB 567, Qal PERFECT (i.e., died in battle)

- has uprooted the enemy's cities, Ps. 9:6 – BDB 684, KB 737, PERFECT

Notice how YHWH is characterized.

- You have maintained my just cause

- You sat on the throne judging righteously

- cf. Ps. 9:7-8 (emphasis repeated in next strophe)

It is possible that "the just cause" is YHWH installing the
psalmist as King of His covenant people.

9:3 "perish before You" Notice
this VERB (BDB 1, KB 2) is repeated in Ps.
9:5, 6, 18. It is used of

- individual enemies

- the nations

- the afflicted (negated)

It obviously refers to physical life but also of eternal existence (cf.
Ps. 9:6, Hebrew idiom). Opposing God and His people is a dangerous
activity with temporal and eschatological consequences.

9:5 "the nations" The same switch
from an individual to "the nations" (cf. Ps. 9:17-20) occurs in
Ps. 7:6-7. Many psalms written by individuals became corporate in worship
liturgy.

Also note that YHWH as Judge is expressed in Ps. 7:7 (cf. Ps. 9:4-6,7-8).

▣ "has blotted out their name forever
and ever" Notice how the theme of "permanent"
judgment is repeated (cf. Ps. 69:28).

- blotted out, Ps. 9:5 (Qal PERFECT,
cf. Ps. 69:28; also note Num. 5:23; Deut. 9:14; 25:19; 29:20)

- forever and ever, Ps. 9:5 (see Special Topic: Forever below)

- perpetual ruins, Ps. 9:6 (Piel PERFECT, cf. Jer. 25:9; 49:13)

- the very memory of them has perished, Ps. 9:6 (Qal PERFECT, cf. Ps. 34:16; 109:15)

Psalm 9:5-6 reminds me of the opening dialog in Malachi 1, where Israel's
very existence is contrasted with the complete demise of Edom as evidence
of YHWH's covenant love. Where are the ancient surrounding nations? They
are lost to history, but not Israel!

The VERB "blot out" (#1) may refer
to the book of life.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('OLAM)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO BOOKS OF GOD

9:7-8 Nations will come and go based on
their relationship to the righteous God/Judge (cf. Ps. 89:14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGE, JUDGMENT, and JUSTICE (שפט)
IN ISAIAH

9:7

NASB
"abides"

NKJV, Peshitta
"endures"

NRSV, TEV, NJB
"sits enthroned"

LXX
"remains"

Psalm 9:7 is in stark contrast to Ps. 9:5-6. The rebellious nations are
temporary but the God of Israel is permanently enthroned (BDB 442, KB 444,
Qal IMPERFECT, cf. Ps. 10:16; 29:10).

The second VERB of Ps. 9:7, "established"
(BDB 465, KB 464), is a Polel PERFECT,
which denotes His permanent throne!

9:8 "He will judge the world in righteousness"
Again the theological issue is the meaning of "world" (BDB 385).
In Ps. 96:13 and 98:9, this word is parallel with erets (BDB 75,
see
Special Topic: Land, Country, Earth). It must refer to the
"known" world of that day. However, from the NT this concept
involves the whole planet (i.e., John 3:16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

9:9 "stronghold" The VERB (BDB 960)
means "to be high." The NOUN is used regularly
of God as a high, mighty, and safe stronghold or fortress (cf. Ps. 9:9 [twice]; 18:2;
46:7,11; 48:3; 59:9,16,17; 62:2,6; 94:22; 144:2). This is an idiom for
safety and protection. For the faithful follower (cf. Ps. 9:10) our God is
our stronghold and there is no other!

▣ "in times of trouble" Notice this phrase of Ps. 9:9b reappears in
Ps. 10:1b. It is found only here in the OT. There is some doubt about the meaning
of the word translated "trouble" (BDB 131). In Jer. 14:1 and 17:8 it means
"drought," but that connotation does not fit here. Remember words have
meaning only in sentences and sentences in literary units.

9:10a This line of poetry expresses a major
biblical reality. I have added my comments from Isa. 26:3-4 below.

For the Hebrew word "know" see

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW.

Isaiah 26:3 "The steadfast of mind You will keep in perfect peace"

- The believer's mind is stayed on YHWH (BDB 701, KB 759, Qal
PASSIVE PARTICIPLE, but used in an ACTIVE
sense, cf. 1 Chr. 29:18).

- YHWH keeps him/her (BDB 665 I, KB 718, Qal IMPERFECT,
the covenant relationship has two participants, see Special Topic at Isaiah 1:19).

- Perfect peace" is a doubling of shalom (BDB 1022, cf. DSS).
This doubling of words is very common in this section of Isaiah.

▣ "he trusts in You" The
word "trust" (BDB 105, KB 120, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE)
means "trust in YHWH" (cf. Isa. 12:2; 26:4; 36:15; 37:10; 50:10). Notice that the
next verse has the same word as an IMPERATIVE. This is such an important
theological concept of the need for a personal relationship with God, not
just obedience. Both are crucial!

26:4 "Trust in the Lord
forever" For the VERB (BDB 105, KB 120, Qal
IMPERATIVE), see

SPECIAL TOPIC: Believe, Trust, Faith, and Faithfulness in the Old Testament.

The name for Deity in the first line of Isa. 26:4 is YHWH; in the second
line a CONTRACTION Yah and YHWH, see

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

The term "forever" (BDB 723 I), first the PLURAL
form and then the SINGULAR form (CNSTRUCT,
cf. Isa. 65:18; Ps. 83:17; 92:8). This construction, along with "everlasting"
(BDB 761), used of YHWH, implies a personal relationship beyond this life (cf. Isa. 26:14,19; Ps. 23:6).

▣ "we have an everlasting rock"
The word "rock" is a metaphor for God's unchanging character
(cf. Ps. 18:1, 2; Isa. 17:10; 30:29; 44:8).

9:10b What a wonderful statement of YHWH's
faithfulness! This is a repeated theme in the Psalms (cf. Ps. 37:28;
94:14). Believers' hope is in the unchanging character of the merciful
Creator (cf. Mal. 3:6).

9:11-12 YHWH is praised because of His
justice (cf. Ps. 9:12,15-16).

- He avenges bloodshed

- He does not forget the cry of the afflicted

His justice is seen in the evil plans by which the wicked have
ensnared themselves (cf. Ps. 9:15-16).

9:11 "who dwells in Zion" Zion is
the hill in Jerusalem on which stood the Jebusite fortress that was
captured by David. He built his palace on this hill. It came to designate
the entire city.

Jerusalem, and particularly the temple on the hill Moriah, became the
place where YHWH "dwelt," between the wings of the Cherubim
above the ark of the covenant. This place fulfills the repeated phrase in
Deuteronomy, "the place that YHWH causes His name to dwell."

This phrase links to Gen. 9:5-6. Life is a gift from God. One who takes

9:13 "the gates of death" Sheol
(see full note at Ps. 6:5) is depicted as

- an open grave/pit (cf. Exod. 15:12; Num. 16:32; 26:10; Ps. 124:3; Prov. 1:12)

- a carnivorous animal (cf. Isa. 5:14; Hab. 2:5)

- a city with gates (cf. Job 38:17; Ps. 107:18; Isa. 38:10; Matt. 16:18)

- a prison with gates (cf. Rev. 1:18; 9:1; 20:1)

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEOL, I. B.

9:14 "in the gates of the daughter of Zion"
There is an obvious contrast between "the gates of death" in Ps.
9:13c and the gates of Jerusalem/temple in Ps. 9:14b. In the first there
is no remembrance but in the second there is praise and testimony about
YHWH.

God's revelation about the afterlife has developed slowly
through Scripture. We call this "progressive revelation." Some doctrines start
in the OT but are not completely revealed until the NT (i.e., "the mystery
hidden from the ages," cf. Eph. 3:4-5). Humans have only a temporal language
linked to this current reality. We do not have the vocabulary or mental ability to
fully grasp the eternal spiritual reality (i.e., 1 Cor. 13:9-12).

One small book that has been a blessing to me in this area
is William Hendriksen's The Bible On the Life Hereafter.

9:15-16 Notice the string of six perfects. The defeat of the enemy army by YWHW
(i.e., Holy War imagery of the Conquest) is the focus.

9:15 Notice the psalmist's adversaries are
nations (cf. Ps. 9:17) and not individuals. Therefore, this must be a
king, so the traditional introduction is probably correct. See Contextual
Insights, A.

9:16 In the OT God's character is manifested
in time by His actions.

- grace, mercy, and love toward covenant people

- judgment and wrath toward their enemies

Notice the reversal of the plans of the wicked. What they planned for
others, occurs to them. Justice is built into God's created order.

This is a study guide commentary, which means
that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of
us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are
priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the
major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be
thought-provoking, not definitive.
